lines: Empty nets at dusk make every rumor sound heavier.
<wavy>Water</wavy> keeps secrets until the weather shakes them loose.
Water looks calm right up until it proves it was thinking.
A good net catches food. A bad net catches excuses.
Weather has more moods than any trader I have met.
Good twine matters. Small failures love important moments.
A snapped line once saved me from hauling in something worse than nothing.
Once the <wavy>fog</wavy> came in so thick I trusted the dock by smell.
An empty net can still bring home a lesson, though nobody cooks it.
Step lightly on the dock. Loose boards like to announce strangers.
Give the dock room. Fishing works better without elbows in it.
Step carefully near the dock. I would rather greet you than patch you up.
A fishing joke needs a good <wavy>line</wavy> and someone patient enough to hear it.
Fishing jokes need timing. Mine usually arrive with water on them.
I keep a spare joke near the dock. It is not always ready for public use.
That insult was damp before it reached me.
I have seen snagged lines with more sense than that.
Careful. Even water looks softer than your manners right now.
I keep space between myself and uncertain weather. People are no different.
Keep your voice even. I am measuring more than your words.
Some questions are safer when they stand a little farther away.
I remember sinking far below myself. You hauled the line in.
The dark had me hooked. You cut the line clean.
You helped pull me back when even my name felt far away.
Your face breaks the surface of that memory, then slips under again.
I remember a taste like bad river water, then breathing like it was new.
The memory is rough around the edges, but your face stayed in it.
I remember you through deep water and panic. Do not crowd the bank.
I know you helped. I also remember why my hands still shake.
The cure left echoes behind. Stand where I can breathe around them.
Thunder shook the barrel so hard the docks creaked under the thunder, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked nets, barrels, and dock posts after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the barrel, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the barrels twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have barrels to set right.
I checked tarred rope and dry dock planks for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the dock planks after.
The nets can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the barrel, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the barrel, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
During a raid, the nets can dry crooked; who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the barrel still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before nets, barrels, and dock posts. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the barrel and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the barrel, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the barrel first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the water past the lanterns and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the barrel enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a coil of rope between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the barrel, though every shadow is being inspected twice.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand out of the barrels.
I checked nets, barrels, and dock posts, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the barrel, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a fisherman which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the barrel, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
The nets can dry crooked. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the barrel found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the barrel. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing ice from the dock edge and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the barrel. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
A clean return, no snags. I like a trip that ends like a well-tied line.
Home again, whole enough to thank you properly. That matters.
We came back with the village still ahead of us. I will count that as good work.
Something got its hook in me out there. Next time, we cut the line sooner.
I made it home, but the road took more from me than it should have.
Next time, let us return with fewer marks and better choices.
I know bait when I see it now. Do not ask me to bite twice.
Following you was trust. What happened after was something else.
A guide who strikes from close by leaves the longest mark.
A boat is honest enough. It goes where it is pointed, unlike some plans.
The boat did its part. I am still deciding whether the rest of the plan did.
Water carried us home, which is more than I expected from that journey.
You taking me by boat was almost sensible. Almost.
That boat trip still sits oddly in my memory, but at least it floated.
A boat can make a bad plan quieter. It cannot make me forget it.
Following you over {follow_distance} blocks felt like reeling in a boot with opinions.
I remember following you through {follow_distance} blocks. My feet remember it even better.
That trip across {follow_distance} blocks taught me to ask more questions before walking.
If we had to cross ocean, at least you used a boat. That is the first sensible part of the story.
That ocean crossing worked because the boat did. I noticed.
The sea made the route look simple. My nerves disagreed.
Swimming across ocean with you was not fishing. It was being the catch.
Crossing ocean water without a boat is not a memory I recommend keeping.
I remember every wave from that crossing, and none of them kindly.
It held steady. Better than most nets, and those are meant to catch trouble.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
Dry, unused, and welcome. Some things should stay out of the water and out of danger.
It did the job when fear was loud. That is praise enough.
Good gear earns trust the moment trouble tests it.
When trouble came in like a bad tide, you helped drag it back out.
A village is a harbor in its own way. You kept ours from burning.
The raid came in rough, and you helped break the current.
You kept the danger from dragging more of us under.
I saw you stand where the tide was meanest.
A safe harbor takes work. Yesterday, you did some.
The village rode out the storm because people held fast.
You helped haul the worst of that night away from our doors.
You cast trouble into the water. Fine. Now reel back something better.
Bad tides pass. I will see whether you bring the same storm again.
You tangled the line. Fine. Untangle it slowly and do not cut it again.
An apology floats. Trust sinks or holds by what follows.
I will hear you out. I have waited longer for worse catches.
Bad waters calm if the wind changes. Let us see whether yours does.
You hooked harm and brought it here. Now bring something decent.
Fine. I will not throw the words back, but I will inspect them.
I have pulled mean things from dark water. Tonight was louder, that is all.
I followed the safest current I could find. Tonight, that current was back here.
I followed the sound of home like a line pulled tight.
Dark water is honest compared to a dark road with raiders near it.
I came back cold, winded, and happy to complain about both.
The night tried to pull me under. I kept my head up.
I have lost catches before. I am glad I was not the catch this time.
The door felt like a dock after bad weather.
Water tells the truth slowly. Trouble splashes faster.
A net catches fish, weeds, secrets, and the occasional reason to stay near shore.
The river is generous if you respect what lives under the shine.
Take {gift_item}. A useful catch should not sit in one pair of hands.
Here, {gift_item}. The water was generous, so I can be too.
Take {gift_item}. It is not much, but it is given with care.
Good. {tested_villager} took {gift_item}; that advice had a clean hook.
Then {gift_item} was the right bait for {tested_villager}. Glad it landed.
Good. {gift_item} suited {tested_villager}; I like advice that holds up.
That line came back empty. For {gift_subject}, cast {alternative_gift} instead.
Some fish spit the hook. Leave {gift_item} and try {alternative_gift} next time.
{gift_item} missed the mark for {gift_subject}. Try {alternative_gift} instead.
Bad bait. It happens. Cast {alternative_gift} if you want a better chance.
Set {gift_item} aside and try {alternative_gift}. This advice should land better.
Then we correct the guess: {alternative_gift} next time.
You took the line, not me. Still, {alternative_gift} should catch better.
Set {gift_item} aside and try {alternative_gift}. This advice should land better.
Then we correct the guess: {alternative_gift} next time.
Mind the dock. What do you need?
Step clear of the dock. What do you need?
Mind the dock; I am listening.
Back to reading water and weather, then.
Back to fishing before the work notices I stopped.
I have line to tend and daylight to spend.
Fine. The line goes slack, for now.
Fine. I will set this down before it gets heavier.
Fine. I can step back, but do not make me regret it.
That offer will not hold. I need {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
That is short of the full repair. Bring {emerald_cost} {emeralds}.
Not enough. It takes {emerald_cost} {emeralds} to settle this.
No. I know when to cut a bad line.
No. Some damage has to cool before payment matters.
No. Keep {payment_items}; trust is not ready to trade.
